entries.note: Rob notes that some Americans prefer to say 'verse' rather than 'versus', and that the episode is really a comparison anyway.
A starter in Britain but the main course in America; the shift came in the early 1900s, possibly by conflating French entrée with [[from?:entre]], 'between'.
Jess points out that [[same-root:entree]] is essentially identical to entry, so it should be the first thing you eat.
Like [[same-root:déjeuner]], it ultimately means to break your fast, but it has moved so far into the day that other words have had to replace it.
Also ultimately means to break your fast; it drifted later in the day to mean lunch, so [[gave:petit déjeuner]] came to be used for breakfast.
Now the French for breakfast, adopted after [[from:déjeuner]] moved later in the day to become lunch.
British phrase that baffles Jess; it means having a shockingly bad day or week, an exaggeration unlike typical British understatement.
An intensifier in American English, which is the original sense from French; British English shifted it to mean only somewhat, so 'quite good' is merely fairly good.
Used by Rob as an American term to admit that Britain changed the meaning of [[see:quite]].
A gentler way of saying no or not precisely, a softening use related to [[see:quite]].
In a YouGov survey most Brits heard it as 'I think you're an idiot', while half of Americans took it as 'I am listening to you'.
Given as a very similar phrase to [[see:with the greatest respect]].
55% of Brits said it meant 'I've forgotten it already', while more Americans took it as sincere; tone can also make it sarcastic.
Brits read it as 'I disagree and don't want to discuss it further'; most Americans took it as accepting the other person's view.
Most Brits see it as mere politeness rather than an invitation; Americans were split between politeness and a genuine invitation to come.
Jess's American parallel to [[see:you must come to dinner]]: a pleasantry that usually means you'll never meet again.
In America it means to get someone pregnant, originally an American sense; regional British usage means to knock on their door, and also to make something.
Film Jess mentions because its title uses the pregnancy sense of [[see:knock someone up]].
Also means a casual game of badminton or tennis; in 17th-century printing, knocking up the balls meant preparing the leather-covered ink balls.
Printing phrase from their printing episode meaning to cover the ink balls in ink; the balls could also be knocked up.
An idiom the hosts invent on the spot, 'having an absolute blusher', modelled on [[see:having a shocker]].
Traditionally 'for a moment' in British English; the later American sense 'in a moment' developed from it.
Irrelevant to Americans but open to debate to Brits; Rob says Americans see it as something debated only in a pretend [[from:moot]].
Traditionally a discussion or debate, like a town hall meeting; law students also hold moots, which are mock trials.
A common American eggcorn for [[see:moot point]], since the American meaning suggests the point might as well be silent.
In America it mainly means betrothed; Brits also use it for an occupied toilet or a busy phone line; from being bound by a pledge, or [[from:gage]].
Jess notes that Americans use it in formal settings to mean an event you have to attend.
The pledge at the root of [[see:engaged]] and [[see:mortgage]]; different French dialects gave English both gage and [[same-root:wage]].
Contains the same [[from:gage]] as [[same-root:engaged]].
Related to [[same-root:gage]]; the two words came into English from different French dialects.
British phrase for mocking someone that baffles Americans; an American Rob met in Morocco thought he meant urinating on her.
A politer form of [[see:taking the piss]], from the Cockney rhyming slang [[from:taking a Mickey Bliss]].
Means angry in American English but drunk in British English.
Rob assumed it was known in the States because he links the name Bob with America, but Jess says it is rarely used there.
The American idiom with uncle, used when you ask someone who is beating you up to stop; Rob had never heard it.
British for 'go away'; its origin is uncertain, but the popular theory is that the hook is an anchor raised before leaving port.
Another way to say [[equivalent:sling your hook]], used in both British and American English.
British phrase meaning going insane or just confused; Jess thought it sounded like internet slang, but Rob says it goes way back.
One of the American baseball idioms Brits might not have; Rob says Britain has now picked them up through American corporate culture.
An American baseball idiom that, Rob says, Brits have now picked up through corporate culture.
An American baseball idiom that has also reached Britain through American corporate culture.
An American football idiom for someone who second-guesses actions afterwards; Rob suggests Britain didn't adopt it because 'quarterback' is too sport-specific.

entries.term: knock it out of the park
entries.note: Rob's example of a sports idiom Brits adopt easily because none of its words are specific to the sport, unlike [[see:Monday morning quarterback]].
American term for a signature, because John Hancock signed the [[see:Declaration of Independence]] in a particularly flamboyant way.
American idiom for being in a difficult position, first recorded in 1923; it may come from [[from?:Kelly pool]] or [[from?:eight-ball pool]].
The British equivalent of [[equivalent:behind the eight ball]], from [[from:snooker]], where the cue ball has no direct shot at a legal ball.
A slogan that was originally an anti-littering campaign, which surprised Rob.
American phrase referring to the Fifth Amendment; Britain has no equivalent amendment, but Rob would understand it from American TV and films.
A Britishism Rob accidentally scripted for Jess in an advert; the American equivalent is [[equivalent:wait in line]].
The American equivalent of [[equivalent:join a queue]].
A Britishism Jess nearly had to say in an advert; it means [[equivalent:shifty]], or [[equivalent:shady]] in American terms.
Rob's gloss for [[equivalent:dodgy]], also used by Americans.
Jess's American equivalent for British [[equivalent:dodgy]].
Jess used it as general online slang without realising it was a Taylor Swift lyric.
Pronounced differently in the two countries; Rob is puzzled that Americans turn a final -os into an 'oh' sound, even in Spanish words.
Whether R is pronounced after vowels, which is a key difference between [[see:General American]] and [[see:Received Pronunciation]]; Rob's non-rhotic accent makes spa and spar identical.
Rob's example of a word he ends with a vowel sound because of non-[[see:rhoticity]].
The generic American accent, sometimes called 'so-called General American', which the hosts compare with [[see:Received Pronunciation]].
RP, the British standard accent, which has had various forms; Rob's own accent is a northern-tinged RP.
Pronounced with and without R as an example of [[see:rhoticity]].
Sounds identical to spa in Rob's non-rhotic accent, though its R is pronounced in sparring; an example of [[see:rhoticity]].
Jess's example of [[see:rhoticity]] after a vowel inside a word.
Rob's example word for comparing rhotic and non-rhotic pronunciation.
Keywords created by [[see:John C. Wells]] in 1982 for comparing the vowels of General American and RP, such as kit, dress, trap, lot, strut and goat.
Linguist whose 1982 book Accents of English created the [[see:lexical sets]].
Lexical-set word whose vowel begins differently in RP and General American, used to illustrate [[see:lexical sets]].
One of Wells's [[see:lexical sets]]; its vowel is merged with those in force and caught in Rob's accent.
Lexical-set word whose vowel Rob pronounces the same as those in north and caught.
Jess pronounces cot and caught the same, while Rob's caught has the same vowel as north and force.
Most American accents merge at least two of Mary, marry and merry; they are distinct in RP, while Jess merges all three.
Example of a two-syllable verb ending in -ate that Americans stress on the first syllable and Brits on the second.
Another example of the stress difference in two-syllable -ate verbs.
Another example of the stress difference in two-syllable -ate verbs.
Example of British clipping of the -ary/-ory ending, which Americans pronounce in full.
Rob calls the British pronunciation classic vowel clipping.
Another -ory word clipped in British English, which Americans overdo when imitating a British accent.
Rob says Brits skip so many letters that it might as well be spelled 'libr'.
An R that non-rhotic speakers slip in between two vowels where none is written, as in [[see:law and order]].
Rob's example of the [[see:intrusive R]].
Along with lost and fog, a word Americans mispronounce in an old-fashioned way when imitating British accents, because the vowel is alien to them.
Example of Americans reducing the ending of -ile words.
Another -ile word whose ending Americans reduce.
Some Americans pronounce it the same as [[same-root?:hostel]], and Rob guesses the two share an origin.
Sounds like [[same-root?:hostile]] for some Americans, which Jess thinks is a double meaning behind the horror franchise [[see:Hostel (film)]].
Horror franchise whose title Jess thinks is a pun on [[see:hostile]].
British phrasing, while Americans say [[equivalent:take a shower]].
American phrasing for the British [[equivalent:have a shower]].
Jess's American phrasing, while Rob would always say [[equivalent:have a bath]].
Rob's British phrasing, as opposed to [[equivalent:take a bath]].
Rob isn't sure whether he would say it or whether it would be American influence; Brits traditionally [[equivalent:sit a test]].
The British phrasing, as opposed to [[equivalent:take a test]].
British phrasing, which even appears in a song; Americans would say [[equivalent:go down to the pub]].
Jess's American phrasing for the British [[equivalent:go down the pub]].
For Jess it need not mean going anywhere, since she could just take one from the fridge; Brits would say going out for a beer.
American phrasing, where British English is more likely to use [[equivalent:see you on Monday]].
British phrasing for the American [[equivalent:see you Monday]].
A British usage that American viewers criticise Rob for; Britain has different to and [[see:different from]], America has [[see:different than]] and different from.
American usage; Jess says critics object because both words are comparative, so the comparison is repeated.
Used on both sides of the Atlantic; Rob finds it the most logical, matching comparatives like [[see:apart from]].
Jess's example of a comparative phrase that takes 'from', supporting [[see:different from]].
Rob's British way of saying he is keen, where Jess says [[equivalent:down for it]].
Jess's American way of saying she is keen, the equivalent of [[equivalent:up for it]].
